questions.question: When a specimen of M25 concrete is loaded to a stress level of 12.5 MPa, a strain of 500×10⁻⁶ is recorded. If this load is allowed to stand for a long time, the strain increases to 1000×10⁻⁶. In accordance with the provisions of IS:456-2000, considering the long-term effects, the effective modulus of elasticity of the concrete (in MPa) is ______
questions.explanation:
Reinforced Concrete Structures | Concrete Properties

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Applied stress level: \(\sigma = 12.5\) MPa
    • Short-term (instantaneous) strain: \(\varepsilon_i = 500 \times 10^{-6}\)
    • Long-term total strain: \(\varepsilon_{\text{total}} = 1000 \times 10^{-6}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the effective modulus of elasticity (\(E_{ce}\)) for the concrete considering long-term effects.

3. Core Concepts:

IS 456:2000 (Clause 6.2.3.1): Accounts for time-dependent deformation (creep) when determining the effective modulus.

\[E_{ce} = \dfrac{E_c}{1 + \theta} \]

where \(\theta\) is the creep coefficient \(\left(\theta = \dfrac{\text{Creep Strain}}{\text{Elastic Strain}}\right)\) and \(E_c\) is the short-term elastic modulus.

Shortcut: \(E_{ce}\) simplifies completely to the applied stress divided by the total accumulated long-term strain.

4. Solution Method:

Divide the applied stress (\(\sigma\)) by the long-term total strain (\(\varepsilon_{\text{total}}\)) to directly obtain \(E_{ce}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify the steady stress and long-term strain:\[\sigma = 12.5\text{ MPa}, \quad \varepsilon_{\text{total}} = 1000 \times 10^{-6} = 0.001 \]
  2. Calculate the effective modulus:\[E_{ce} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{\text{total}}} = \dfrac{12.5}{0.001} = 12500\text{ MPa} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 12500 MPa | Accepted key range: 12500 to 12500

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q40
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A water treatment plant treats 6000 m³ of water per day. As a part of the treatment process, discrete particles are required to be settled in a clarifier. A column test indicates that an overflow rate of 1.5 m per hour would produce the desired removal of particles through settling in the clarifier having a depth of 3.0 m. The volume of the required clarifier, (in m³, round off to 1 decimal place) would be ______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Plant flow rate: \(Q = 6000\) m³/day
    • Surface Overflow Rate (SOR): \(v_o = 1.5\) m/hour
    • Clarifier depth: \(H = 3.0\) m
  • Aim: Compute the required total volume of the clarifier.

3. Core Concepts:

Clarifier Surface Area: Governed purely by flow and overflow rate:

\[A = \dfrac{Q}{v_o} \]

Volume:

\[V = A \times H \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Standardize units: Convert daily flow rate \(Q\) into an hourly rate so it aligns with \(v_o\).
  2. Compute the required plan area \(A\).
  3. Multiply \(A\) by the required depth \(H\) to find the volume.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Flow rate conversion:\[Q = \dfrac{6000\text{ m}^3/\text{day}}{24\text{ hours/day}} = 250\text{ m}^3/\text{hour} \]
  2. Calculate Plan Area (\(A\)):\[A = \dfrac{Q}{v_o} = \dfrac{250\text{ m}^3/\text{hour}}{1.5\text{ m/hour}} = 166.667\text{ m}^2 \]
  3. Calculate Volume (\(V\)):\[V = A \times H = 166.667\text{ m}^2 \times 3.0\text{ m} = 500.0\text{ m}^3 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 500.0 m³ | Accepted key range: 495.0 to 505.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
Raw municipal solid waste (MSW) collected from a city contains 70% decomposable material that can be converted to methane. The water content of the decomposable material is 35%. An elemental analysis of the decomposable material yields the following mass percent.
C : H : O : N : other = 44 : 6 : 43 : 0.8 : 6.2

The methane production of the decomposable material is governed by the following stoichiometric relation
CₐHO꜀Nₔ + nH₂O → mCH₄ + sCO₂ + dNH₃

Given atomic weights: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, N = 14. The mass of methane produced (in grams, round off to 1 decimal place) per kg of raw MSW will be ______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Solid Waste Management

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Raw MSW mass base: 1 kg (1000 g)
    • Decomposable fraction: 70%
    • Moisture content in decomposable fraction: 35%
    • Elemental composition (on dry mass basis): C = 44%, H = 6%, O = 43%, N = 0.8%, Ash/Other = 6.2%
    • Reaction: \(C_a H_b O_c N_d + nH_2O \rightarrow mCH_4 + sCO_2 + dNH_3\)
  • Aim: Calculate the mass of methane (\(CH_4\)) produced (in grams) per 1 kg of raw MSW.

3. Core Concepts:

Moisture Content Adjustment: Elemental percentages are strictly given for the dry mass of solid waste.

Stoichiometry of Anaerobic Digestion: Balancing the carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen dictates the theoretical maximum methane yield. General stoichiometric formula:

\[m = \dfrac{4a + b - 2c - 3d}{8} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the actual dry mass of decomposable material available in 1 kg of raw MSW.
  2. Formulate the mole proportions for a 100 g chunk of the dry material to find coefficients \(a, b, c, d\).
  3. Substitute moles into the digestion stoichiometric equation to find the moles of \(CH_4\) produced.
  4. Scale up the \(CH_4\) mass yield from the 100 g sample to the full dry decomposable mass.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Mass Extraction:
    • Raw MSW \(= 1000\) g
    • Wet Decomposable Material \(= 0.70 \times 1000 = 700\) g
    • Dry Decomposable Material \(= 700 \times (1 - 0.35) = 455\) g
  2. Mole Coefficients (\(a, b, c, d\)) per 100 g dry material:
    • \(a\) (Carbon) \(= \dfrac{44}{12} = 3.6667\) mol
    • \(b\) (Hydrogen) \(= \dfrac{6}{1} = 6.0000\) mol
    • \(c\) (Oxygen) \(= \dfrac{43}{16} = 2.6875\) mol
    • \(d\) (Nitrogen) \(= \dfrac{0.8}{14} = 0.0571\) mol
  3. Methane yield (\(m\)) per 100 g of dry material:\[m = \dfrac{4(3.6667) + 6.0000 - 2(2.6875) - 3(0.0571)}{8} \]\[m = \dfrac{14.6668 + 6.0000 - 5.3750 - 0.1713}{8} = \dfrac{15.1205}{8} = 1.890\text{ mol of }CH_4 \]
  4. Scale to total mass (455 g):
    • Mass of \(CH_4\) per 100 g dry \(= 1.890 \times 16 = 30.24\) g
    • Total \(CH_4\) from 1 kg MSW \(= 30.24 \times \dfrac{455}{100} = 137.59\) g

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 137.6 g | Accepted key range: 135.0 to 140.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Consider the reactor shown in the figure. The flow rate through the reactor is Q m³/h. The concentrations (in mg/L) of a compound in the influent and effluent are C₀ and C, respectively. The compound is degraded in the reactor following the first order reaction. The mixing condition of the reactor can be varied such that the reactor becomes either a completely mixed flow reactor (CMFR) or a plug-flow reactor (PFR). The length of the reactor can be adjusted in these two mixing conditions to L_CMFR and L_PFR while keeping the cross-section of the reactor constant. Assuming steady state and for C/C₀ = 0.8, the value of L_CMFR/L_PFR (round off to 2 decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Treatment Kinetics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Constant reactor cross-section: \(A\)
    • First order decay reaction constant: \(k\)
    • Removal efficiency target: \(C/C_0 = 0.8\)
  • Aim: Evaluate the ratio \(L_{CMFR} / L_{PFR}\) for the required lengths of Completely Mixed Flow Reactor (CMFR) and Plug-Flow Reactor (PFR).

3. Core Concepts:

CMFR Performance Equation: Based on a single mixed macroscopic mass balance:

\[V_{CMFR} = \dfrac{Q}{k} \left(\dfrac{C_0}{C} - 1\right) \]

PFR Performance Equation: Follows integrated differential mass balance, identical functionally to batch reactors:

\[V_{PFR} = \dfrac{Q}{k} \ln\left(\dfrac{C_0}{C}\right) \]

For constant flow \(Q\) and equal cross-sectional areas (\(V = A \times L\)), the lengths scale proportionally to respective volumetric requirements.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Isolate the \(C_0/C\) term from the target remaining concentration factor.
  2. Construct parametric equations for both \(L_{CMFR}\) and \(L_{PFR}\).
  3. Divide the expressions to get a clean ratio that cancels out \(Q\), \(A\), and \(k\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate the required inverse reduction factor:\[\dfrac{C}{C_0} = 0.8 \implies \dfrac{C_0}{C} = \dfrac{1}{0.8} = 1.25 \]
  2. Formulate reactor length expressions using \(L = V/A\):
    • For CMFR:\[L_{CMFR} = \dfrac{Q}{A \cdot k} \left(\dfrac{C_0}{C} - 1\right) = \dfrac{Q}{A \cdot k}(1.25 - 1) = \dfrac{0.25\,Q}{A \cdot k} \]
    • For PFR:\[L_{PFR} = \dfrac{Q}{A \cdot k} \ln\left(\dfrac{C_0}{C}\right) = \dfrac{Q}{A \cdot k} \ln(1.25) \approx \dfrac{0.22314\,Q}{A \cdot k} \]
  3. Calculate ratio \(L_{CMFR}/L_{PFR}\):\[\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{0.25}{\ln(1.25)} = \dfrac{0.25}{0.22314} = 1.1203 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.12 | Accepted key range: 1.10 to 1.15

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: A series of perpendicular offsets taken from a curved boundary wall to a straight survey line at an interval of 6 m are 1.22, 1.67, 2.04, 2.34, 2.14, 1.87, and 1.15 m. The area (in m², round off to 2 decimal places) bounded by the survey line, curved boundary wall, the first and the last offsets, determined using Simpson’s rule, is ______
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Area & Volume Computations

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Series of perpendicular offsets: \(O_1 = 1.22\) m, \(O_2 = 1.67\) m, \(O_3 = 2.04\) m, \(O_4 = 2.34\) m, \(O_5 = 2.14\) m, \(O_6 = 1.87\) m, \(O_7 = 1.15\) m
    • Interval between offsets (\(d\)): 6 m
    • Total number of offsets (\(n\)): 7
  • Aim: Calculate the total area using Simpson's rule, rounded to 2 decimal places.

3. Core Concepts:

Simpson's One-Third Rule: Used to determine the area of irregular tracts. It assumes the boundary between consecutive offset intervals is a parabolic arc.

\[ \text{Area} = \dfrac{d}{3}\left[(O_1 + O_n) + 4(O_2 + O_4 + \dots + O_{n-1}) + 2(O_3 + O_5 + \dots + O_{n-2})\right] \]

Condition for Application: The rule is strictly applicable only when the total number of offsets (\(n\)) is odd (i.e., the number of intervals is even). Here \(n = 7\), so the condition is satisfied perfectly.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Verify the number of offsets is odd.
  2. Group the offsets into: first & last, even-numbered, and remaining odd-numbered.
  3. Compute the sum of each group.
  4. Apply Simpson's one-third rule formula to find the total area.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Identify and categorize offsets
    • \(d = 6\) m
    • First and Last: \(O_1 = 1.22\) m, \(O_7 = 1.15\) m
    • Even-indexed: \(O_2 = 1.67\) m, \(O_4 = 2.34\) m, \(O_6 = 1.87\) m
    • Odd-indexed (excluding first and last): \(O_3 = 2.04\) m, \(O_5 = 2.14\) m
  2. Step 2: Calculate subgroup sums
    • \((O_1 + O_7) = 1.22 + 1.15 = 2.37\) m
    • \((O_2 + O_4 + O_6) = 1.67 + 2.34 + 1.87 = 5.88\) m
    • \((O_3 + O_5) = 2.04 + 2.14 = 4.18\) m
  3. Step 3: Apply Simpson's Rule\[ \text{Area} = \dfrac{6}{3} \times [2.37 + 4(5.88) + 2(4.18)] \]\[ = 2 \times [2.37 + 23.52 + 8.36] = 2 \times 34.25 = 68.50\text{ m}^2 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 68.50 m² | Accepted key range: 67.00 to 70.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q44
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: The uniform arrival and uniform service rates observed on an approach road to a signalized intersection are 20 and 50 vehicles/minute, respectively. For this signal, the red time is 30 s, the effective green time is 30 s, and the cycle length is 60 s. Assuming that initially there are no vehicles in the queue, the average delay per vehicle using the approach road during a cycle length (in s, round off to 2 decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Signals (Queuing Theory)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Arrival rate (\(q\)): 20 veh/min
    • Service rate (\(s\)): 50 veh/min
    • Red time (\(r\)): 30 s
    • Effective green time (\(g\)): 30 s
    • Cycle length (\(C\)): 60 s
    • Initial queue: 0 vehicles
  • Aim: Calculate the average delay per vehicle (in seconds) during one cycle length.

3. Core Concepts:

Deterministic Queuing at Signals: Since arrival and service rates are uniform, random delay components are zero. The delay is entirely "uniform delay", found by evaluating the area of the queue accumulation polygon (a triangle).

Variables in standard units (veh/sec):

  • \(q = \dfrac{20}{60} = \dfrac{1}{3}\) veh/s
  • \(s = \dfrac{50}{60} = \dfrac{5}{6}\) veh/s

Total Delay (\(D\)): Area of the queue triangle \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times (\text{Time queue exists}) \times (\text{Maximum queue})\)

Webster's Uniform Delay Formula (Alternative):

\[d_1 = \dfrac{C(1 - \lambda)^2}{2(1 - \lambda x)} \]

where \(\lambda = g/C\) and \(x = q/(\lambda s)\) (Degree of saturation).

4. Solution Method (Queue Polygon Method):

  1. Convert rates from veh/min to veh/s.
  2. Find the maximum queue length built up during the red phase.
  3. Calculate the time required to clear this queue during the green phase.
  4. Find the total delay (area of the queue-time triangle).
  5. Divide total delay by the total number of vehicles arriving in the cycle.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Conversion of units
    \(q = 20/60 = 0.333\) veh/s, \(s = 50/60 = 0.833\) veh/s
  2. Step 2: Queue buildup during Red time (\(r = 30\) s)\[Q_{\text{max}} = q \times r = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 30 = 10\text{ vehicles} \]
  3. Step 3: Queue dissipation during Green time
    Net discharge rate \(= s - q\). Time to clear queue:\[t_c = \dfrac{Q_{\text{max}}}{s - q} = \dfrac{10}{\dfrac{5}{6} - \dfrac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{10}{0.5} = 20\text{ s} \]Sanity Check: \(t_c\) (20 s) < Effective green time (30 s). Queue clears before green ends.
  4. Step 4: Total uniform delay (\(D\))
    Total time queue exists \(= r + t_c = 30 + 20 = 50\) s\[D = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 50\text{ s} \times 10\text{ veh} = 250\text{ veh-s} \]
  5. Step 5: Average delay per vehicle
    Total vehicles in one cycle \(= q \times C = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 60 = 20\) vehicles\[\text{Average delay} = \dfrac{250\text{ veh-s}}{20\text{ veh}} = 12.5\text{ s/veh} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 12.50 s/veh | Accepted key range: 12.00 to 13.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q45
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A broad gauge railway line passes through a horizontal curved section (radius = 875 m) of length 200 m. The allowable speed on this portion is 100 km/h. For calculating the cant, consider the gauge as centre-to-centre distance between the rail heads, equal to 1750 mm. The maximum permissible cant (in mm, round off to 1 decimal place) with respect to the centre-to-centre distance between the rail heads is ______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Railway Geometric Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Radius of curve (\(R\)): 875 m
    • Length of curve (\(L\)): 200 m (Distractor data)
    • Allowable speed (\(V\)): 100 km/h
    • Gauge (\(G\)): 1750 mm = 1.750 m (Centre-to-centre distance between rail heads)
  • Aim: Determine the maximum permissible (equilibrium) cant in mm, rounded to 1 decimal place.

3. Core Concepts:

Superelevation (Cant): The elevation of the outer rail above the inner rail at a horizontal curve to counteract centrifugal force.

Equilibrium Cant Formula: Derived from basic mechanics where centrifugal force is balanced by the gravity component of the canted track.

\[e = \dfrac{G \cdot v^2}{g \cdot R} \]

Where \(v\) is speed in m/s, \(g = 9.81\) m/s².

Standard Engineering Practical Formula: By substituting \(v = V/3.6\):

\[e = \dfrac{G \cdot V^2}{127 \cdot R} \]

(Using exactly \(g = 9.81\) gives a denominator constant of 127.14, but 127 is the standard code-adopted constant in India.)

4. Solution Method:

Apply the exact equilibrium cant formula, keeping \(G\) in mm to obtain \(e\) directly in mm.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Method 1: Exact Fundamental Calculation (\(g = 9.81\) m/s²)

  1. Convert speed to m/s: \(v = 100 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 27.778\) m/s
  2. Substitute into equilibrium equation:\[e = \dfrac{1750\text{ mm} \times (27.778)^2}{9.81 \times 875} = \dfrac{1750 \times 771.605}{8583.75} = 157.31\text{ mm} \]

Method 2: Using standard codal constant (127)

\[e = \dfrac{G \cdot V^2}{127 \cdot R} = \dfrac{1750 \times (100)^2}{127 \times 875} = \dfrac{17{,}500{,}000}{111{,}125} = 157.48\text{ mm} \]

Both 157.3 and 157.5 fall within the GATE official accepted range. The rigorously calculated fundamental answer is 157.3 mm.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 157.3 mm | Accepted key range: 157.3 to 157.6

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
The speed-density relationship of a highway is given as

\[u = 100 - 0.5k\]

where, \(u\) = speed in km per hour, \(k\) = density in vehicles per km. The maximum flow (in vehicles per hour, round off to the nearest integer) is ______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Flow Models

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Speed-density relationship: \(u = 100 - 0.5k\)
    • \(u\) = speed in km/h, \(k\) = density in vehicles/km
  • Aim: Calculate the maximum flow (\(q_{\text{max}}\)) in vehicles per hour.

3. Core Concepts:

Fundamental Traffic Equation:

\[q = u \cdot k \]

Greenshields Macroscopic Model: Assumes a linear relationship between speed and density.

\[u = u_f \left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right) \]

Where \(u_f\) is free-flow speed and \(k_j\) is jam density.

Maximum Flow (\(q_{\text{max}}\)): Occurs at exactly half the free-flow speed and half the jam density (vertex of the flow-density parabola):

\[q_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{u_f \cdot k_j}{4} \]

4. Solution Method:

Method A (Direct Formula): Map the given equation to Greenshields format to extract \(u_f\) and \(k_j\), then use the \(q_{\text{max}}\) formula.

Method B (Calculus — First Principles): Express flow as a function of density, differentiate, and equate to zero.

5. Step-by-Step Execution (First Principles):

  1. Step 1: Setup flow equation\[q = u \cdot k = (100 - 0.5k) \cdot k = 100k - 0.5k^2 \]
  2. Step 2: Maximize flow
    Take the derivative of \(q\) with respect to \(k\) and set it to 0:\[\dfrac{dq}{dk} = 100 - k = 0 \implies k = 100\text{ veh/km} \](This is the optimum density \(k_0\) — exactly half the jam density \(k_j = 200\).)
  3. Step 3: Calculate maximum flow\[q_{\text{max}} = 100(100) - 0.5(100)^2 = 10000 - 5000 = 5000\text{ veh/h} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 5000 veh/h | Accepted key range: 5000 to 5000

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A confined aquifer of 15 m constant thickness is sandwiched between two aquicludes as shown in the figure (not drawn to scale).


The heads indicated by two piezometers P and Q are 55.2 m and 34.1 m, respectively. The aquifer has a hydraulic conductivity of 80 m/day and its effective porosity is 0.25. If the distance between the piezometers is 2500 m, the time taken by the water to travel through the aquifer from piezometer location P to Q (in days, round off to 1 decimal place) is ______
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Groundwater Hydrology

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Aquifer thickness (\(b\)): 15 m (Distractor)
    • Piezometric head at P (\(h_P\)): 55.2 m
    • Piezometric head at Q (\(h_Q\)): 34.1 m
    • Distance between P and Q (\(L\)): 2500 m
    • Hydraulic conductivity (\(K\)): 80 m/day
    • Effective porosity (\(n_e\)): 0.25
  • Aim: Calculate the actual travel time of water from P to Q in days, rounded to 1 decimal place.

3. Core Concepts:

Darcy's Law: Gives the apparent (discharge) velocity \(v\) of water through a porous medium.

\[v = K \cdot i \quad \left(i = \dfrac{\Delta h}{L}\right) \]

Seepage Velocity (True Velocity): Water only travels through the void spaces, so the actual travel speed \(v_s\) is faster than Darcy's velocity.

\[v_s = \dfrac{v}{n_e} \]

Travel Time (\(t\)):

\[t = \dfrac{L}{v_s} \]

Note: The aquifer thickness (15 m) dictates total discharge but is completely irrelevant for evaluating particle travel time.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the head difference (\(\Delta h\)) between the two piezometers.
  2. Compute the hydraulic gradient (\(i\)).
  3. Calculate the Darcy velocity (\(v\)).
  4. Calculate the Seepage velocity (\(v_s\)) using the effective porosity.
  5. Find the travel time by dividing the total length by the seepage velocity.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate Hydraulic Gradient (\(i\))\[\Delta h = h_P - h_Q = 55.2 - 34.1 = 21.1\text{ m} \]\[i = \dfrac{\Delta h}{L} = \dfrac{21.1}{2500} = 0.00844 \]
  2. Step 2: Calculate Darcy Velocity (\(v\))\[v = K \cdot i = 80 \times 0.00844 = 0.6752\text{ m/day} \]
  3. Step 3: Calculate Seepage Velocity (\(v_s\))\[v_s = \dfrac{v}{n_e} = \dfrac{0.6752}{0.25} = 2.7008\text{ m/day} \]
  4. Step 4: Calculate Travel Time (\(t\))\[t = \dfrac{L}{v_s} = \dfrac{2500}{2.7008} = 925.651\text{ days} \approx 925.7\text{ days} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 925.7 days | Accepted key range: 924.0 to 926.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
At the foot of a spillway, water flows at a depth of 23 cm with a velocity of 8.1 m/s, as shown in the figure.


The flow enters as an M-3 profile in the long wide rectangular channel with bed slope = \(\dfrac{1}{1800}\) and Manning’s n = 0.015. A hydraulic jump is formed at a certain distance from the foot of the spillway. Assume the acceleration due to gravity, g = 9.81 m/s². Just before the hydraulic jump, the depth of flow y₁ (in m, round off to 2 decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow (Hydraulic Jump)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Initial depth of flow, \(y_0 = 23\) cm \(= 0.23\) m
    • Initial velocity, \(V_0 = 8.1\) m/s
    • Bed slope, \(S_0 = 1/1800\)
    • Manning's roughness coefficient, \(n = 0.015\)
    • \(g = 9.81\) m/s²
    • Channel type: Long, wide rectangular channel
    • Profile type: M-3 profile (mild slope, supercritical flow)
  • Aim: Find the depth of flow just before the hydraulic jump, \(y_1\).

3. Core Concepts:

Specific Discharge (\(q\)): For a wide rectangular channel, \(q = V_0 y_0\).

Normal Depth (\(y_n\)): The depth the flow will eventually try to reach. Calculated using Manning's equation for a wide channel (\(R \approx y\)):

\[q = \dfrac{1}{n} y_n^{5/3} S_0^{1/2} \]

Hydraulic Jump Conjugate Depths:

\[\dfrac{2q^2}{g} = y_1 y_2 (y_1 + y_2) \]

Jump Location Condition: In an M-3 profile on a long mild slope, the depth after the jump must equal the normal depth: \(y_2 = y_n\).

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate specific discharge (\(q\))\[q = V_0 \times y_0 = 8.1 \times 0.23 = 1.863\text{ m}^2\text{/s/m} \]
  2. Step 2: Determine normal depth (\(y_n\))\[1.863 = \dfrac{1}{0.015} y_n^{5/3} \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{1800}} = 66.667 \times \dfrac{1}{42.426} \cdot y_n^{5/3} = 1.5714\, y_n^{5/3} \]\[y_n^{5/3} = \dfrac{1.863}{1.5714} = 1.1856 \implies y_n = (1.1856)^{3/5} = 1.107\text{ m} \]
  3. Step 3: Solve for depth before the jump (\(y_1\))
    With \(y_2 = y_n = 1.107\) m, using the conjugate depths relation:\[\dfrac{2 \times (1.863)^2}{9.81} = y_1 (1.107)(y_1 + 1.107) \]\[0.7076 = 1.107 y_1^2 + 1.225 y_1 \]Rearranging:\[1.107 y_1^2 + 1.225 y_1 - 0.7076 = 0 \]Solving using the quadratic formula:\[y_1 = \dfrac{-1.225 + \sqrt{(1.225)^2 + 4(1.107)(0.7076)}}{2 \times 1.107} = \dfrac{-1.225 + \sqrt{4.6338}}{2.214} = \dfrac{0.9276}{2.214} = 0.419\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.42 m | Accepted key range: 0.41 to 0.43

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: Two identical pipes (i.e., having the same length, same diameter, and same roughness) are used to withdraw water from a reservoir. In the first case, they are attached in series and discharge freely into the atmosphere. In the second case, they are attached in parallel and also discharge freely into the atmosphere. Neglecting all minor losses, and assuming that the friction factor is same in both the cases, the ratio of the discharge in the parallel arrangement to that in the series arrangement (round off to 2 decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Flow (Pipes in Series and Parallel)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Two identical pipes: Length \(L\), Diameter \(D\), Friction factor \(f\)
    • Case 1: Attached in Series. Discharge \(= Q_s\)
    • Case 2: Attached in Parallel. Discharge \(= Q_p\)
    • Both cases withdraw from the same reservoir under constant head \(H\). Minor losses neglected.
  • Aim: Ratio of discharge \(Q_p / Q_s\).

3. Core Concepts:

Darcy-Weisbach Equation: In terms of discharge \(Q\):

\[h_f = \dfrac{8 f L Q^2}{\pi^2 g D^5} = k L Q^2 \]

where \(k = \dfrac{8f}{\pi^2 g D^5}\) is a constant for identical pipes.

Series Arrangement: Total head loss is the sum of individual pipe losses. Discharge \(Q_s\) is uniform throughout.

Parallel Arrangement: Head loss across each pipe equals \(H\). Total discharge \(Q_p\) is the sum of individual branch discharges.

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Series Case\[H = kLQ_s^2 + kLQ_s^2 = 2kLQ_s^2 \implies Q_s = \sqrt{\dfrac{H}{2kL}} \]
  2. Step 2: Parallel Case
    Head loss in each branch:\[H = kLQ_{p1}^2 \implies Q_{p1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{H}{kL}} \]Total discharge:\[Q_p = 2Q_{p1} = 2\sqrt{\dfrac{H}{kL}} \]
  3. Step 3: Calculate the Ratio\[\dfrac{Q_p}{Q_s} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{\dfrac{H}{kL}}}{\sqrt{\dfrac{H}{2kL}}} = \dfrac{2}{1/\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2} = 2 \times 1.414 = 2.828 \approx 2.83 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.83 | Accepted key range: 2.80 to 2.90

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The ordinates, u, of a 2-hour unit hydrograph (i.e., for 1 cm of effective rain), for a catchment are shown in the table.
t (hour)0123456789101112
u (m³/s)0281832453019127310

A 6-hour storm occurs over the catchment such that the effective rainfall intensity is 1 cm/hour for the first two hours, zero for the next two hours, and 0.5 cm/hour for the last two hours. If the base flow is constant at 5 m³/s, the peak flow due to this storm (in m³/s, round off to 1 decimal place) will be ______
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Hydrographs (Unit Hydrograph)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Ordinates of a 2-hour Unit Hydrograph (UH) for 1 cm effective rain
    • Base flow \(= 5\) m³/s (constant)
    • 6-hour storm (in 2-hour blocks):
      • 0–2 hr: Intensity \(i_1 = 1\) cm/h
      • 2–4 hr: Intensity \(i_2 = 0\) cm/h
      • 4–6 hr: Intensity \(i_3 = 0.5\) cm/h
  • Aim: Find the peak flow (Total Discharge) due to this storm.

3. Core Concepts:

Effective Rainfall (ER): \(ER = \text{Intensity} \times \text{Duration}\)

Superposition Principle: The Direct Runoff Hydrograph (DRH) is obtained by multiplying each ER depth with the shifted UH ordinates and summing them.

Total Flow: Peak Flow = Maximum DRH + Base Flow.

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate Effective Rainfall (ER) for each 2-hour block
    • \(ER_1\) (0–2 hr) \(= 1 \times 2 = 2\) cm
    • \(ER_2\) (2–4 hr) \(= 0 \times 2 = 0\) cm
    • \(ER_3\) (4–6 hr) \(= 0.5 \times 2 = 1\) cm
  2. Step 2: Superimpose the Unit Hydrograph ordinates\[DR(t) = ER_1 \cdot U(t) + ER_2 \cdot U(t-2) + ER_3 \cdot U(t-4) = 2\,U(t) + 0 + 1\,U(t-4) \]
  3. Step 3: Tabulate combined DRH ordinates around the peak
    Time (hr)\(2 \cdot U(t)\)\(1 \cdot U(t-4)\)DR(t) (m³/s)
    42(32) = 641(0) = 064
    52(45) = 901(2) = 292
    62(30) = 601(8) = 868
    72(19) = 381(18) = 1856
    82(12) = 241(32) = 3256
    92(7) = 141(45) = 4559
    Maximum direct runoff \(= 92\) m³/s at \(t = 5\) hours.
  4. Step 4: Calculate Peak Flow\[\text{Peak Flow} = 92 + 5 = 97\text{ m}^3\text{/s} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 97.0 m³/s | Accepted key range: 96.5 to 97.5

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
The dimensions of a soil sampler are given in the table.
ParameterCutting edgeSampling tube
Inside diameter (mm)8086

For this sampler, the outside clearance ratio (in percent, round off to 2 decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Exploration (Sampler Design)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Cutting edge inner diameter, \(D_1 = 80\) mm
    • Cutting edge outer diameter, \(D_2 = 100\) mm
    • Sampling tube inner diameter, \(D_3 = 86\) mm
    • Sampling tube outer diameter, \(D_4 = 90\) mm
  • Aim: Calculate the outside clearance ratio (in percent).

3. Core Concepts:

Outside Clearance Ratio (\(C_o\)): Reduces driving friction between the outer surface of the sampler and the soil. It is calculated as:

\[C_o (\%) = \dfrac{D_2 - D_4}{D_4} \times 100 \]

Where \(D_2\) is the outer diameter of the cutting edge (shoe) and \(D_4\) is the outer diameter of the sampling tube.

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

Substitute the corresponding outer diameter values into the standard formula:

\[C_o = \dfrac{100 - 90}{90} \times 100 = \dfrac{10}{90} \times 100 = 11.11\% \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 11.11% | Accepted key range: 11.10 to 11.12

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A 2 m × 4 m rectangular footing has to carry a uniformly distributed load of 120 kPa. As per the 2:1 dispersion method of stress distribution, the increment in vertical stress (in kPa) at a depth of 2 m below the footing is ______
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Stress Distribution

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Rectangular footing dimensions: \(B = 2\) m, \(L = 4\) m
    • Uniformly distributed load: \(q = 120\) kPa
    • Target depth: \(z = 2\) m
  • Aim: Determine the increment in vertical stress (\(\Delta\sigma_z\)) at depth \(z = 2\) m using the 2:1 dispersion method.

3. Core Concepts:

2:1 Dispersion Method: Assumes the applied load spreads at a slope of 2 Vertical to 1 Horizontal. The loaded area increases by \(z/2\) on all four sides at depth \(z\). Equivalent dimensions become \((B + z)\) and \((L + z)\).

\[\Delta\sigma_z = \dfrac{Q}{(B+z)(L+z)} \quad \text{where } Q = q \times B \times L \]

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate total applied load (\(Q\))\[Q = 120 \times 2 \times 4 = 960\text{ kN} \]
  2. Step 2: Calculate dispersed area dimensions at depth \(z = 2\) m\[B_z = B + z = 2 + 2 = 4\text{ m}, \quad L_z = L + z = 4 + 2 = 6\text{ m} \]\[A_z = 4 \times 6 = 24\text{ m}^2 \]
  3. Step 3: Calculate increment in vertical stress\[\Delta\sigma_z = \dfrac{960}{24} = 40\text{ kPa} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 40 kPa | Accepted key range: 40 to 40

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: Constant head permeability tests were performed on two soil specimens, S1 and S2. The ratio of height of the two specimens (L_S1:L_S2) is 1.5, the ratio of the diameter of specimens (D_S1:D_S2) is 0.5, and the ratio of the constant head (h_S1:h_S2) applied on the specimens is 2.0. If the discharge from both the specimens is equal, the ratio of the permeability of the soil specimens (k_S1:k_S2) is ______
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Permeability

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Ratio of specimen heights: \(L_{S1}/L_{S2} = 1.5\)
    • Ratio of specimen diameters: \(D_{S1}/D_{S2} = 0.5\)
    • Ratio of constant heads: \(h_{S1}/h_{S2} = 2.0\)
    • Equal discharge: \(Q_{S1} = Q_{S2}\)
  • Aim: Ratio of permeability coefficients, \(k_{S1}/k_{S2}\).

3. Core Concepts:

Darcy's Law for Constant Head Test:

\[Q = k \cdot i \cdot A = k \left(\dfrac{h}{L}\right) \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} D^2\right) \]

Rearranging to solve for permeability \(k\):

\[k = \dfrac{4 \cdot Q \cdot L}{\pi \cdot h \cdot D^2} \]

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Formulate the ratio equation
    Since \(Q\) and \(\pi/4\) are constants for both setups, \(k \propto L / (h \cdot D^2)\):\[\dfrac{k_{S1}}{k_{S2}} = \left(\dfrac{L_{S1}}{L_{S2}}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{h_{S2}}{h_{S1}}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{D_{S2}}{D_{S1}}\right)^2 \]
  2. Step 2: Substitute given ratios
    • \(L_{S1}/L_{S2} = 1.5\)
    • \(h_{S2}/h_{S1} = 1/2.0 = 0.5\)
    • \(D_{S2}/D_{S1} = 1/0.5 = 2.0\)
  3. Step 3: Compute final ratio\[\dfrac{k_{S1}}{k_{S2}} = 1.5 \times 0.5 \times (2.0)^2 = 0.75 \times 4 = 3.0 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3 | Accepted key range: 3 to 3

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A timber pile of length 8 m and diameter 0.2 m is driven with a 20 kN drop hammer, falling freely from a height of 1.5 m. The total penetration of the pile in the last 5 blows is 40 mm. Use the Engineering News Record expression. Assume a factor of safety of 6 and empirical factor (allowing reduction in the theoretical set, due to energy losses) of 2.5 cm. The safe load carrying capacity of the pile (in kN, round off to 2 decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Deep Foundations (Pile Capacity)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Timber pile: Length \(L = 8\) m, Diameter \(D = 0.2\) m
    • Drop hammer weight, \(W = 20\) kN
    • Height of fall, \(H = 1.5\) m \(= 150\) cm
    • Total penetration for last 5 blows \(= 40\) mm \(= 4\) cm
    • Factor of Safety, \(FOS = 6\)
    • Empirical constant for drop hammer, \(C = 2.5\) cm
  • Aim: Safe load carrying capacity of the pile (\(Q_s\)) in kN.

3. Core Concepts:

Engineering News Record (ENR) Formula: Used for calculating the ultimate load capacity (\(Q_u\)) of driven piles based on driving resistance.

\[Q_u = \dfrac{W \cdot H}{S + C} \]

Unit consistency is critical! When \(H\), \(S\), and \(C\) are all in cm, the result \(Q_u\) shares the unit of \(W\) (kN).

Set per blow (\(S\)): Average penetration per blow over the last few blows.

Safe Load: \(Q_s = Q_u / FOS\)

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate the Set per blow (\(S\))\[S = \dfrac{40\text{ mm}}{5\text{ blows}} = 8\text{ mm/blow} = 0.8\text{ cm/blow} \]
  2. Step 2: Calculate Ultimate Load (\(Q_u\))\[Q_u = \dfrac{20\text{ kN} \times 150\text{ cm}}{0.8\text{ cm} + 2.5\text{ cm}} = \dfrac{3000}{3.3} = 909.09\text{ kN} \]
  3. Step 3: Calculate Safe Load (\(Q_s\))\[Q_s = \dfrac{909.09}{6} = 151.52\text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 151.52 kN | Accepted key range: 151.00 to 152.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A square footing of 2 m sides rests on the surface of a homogeneous soil bed having the properties: cohesion c = 24 kPa, angle of internal friction φ = 25°, and unit weight γ = 18 kN/m³. Terzaghi’s bearing capacity factors for φ = 25° are N_c = 25.1, N_q = 12.7, N_γ = 9.7, N_c' = 14.8, N_q' = 5.6, and N_γ' = 3.2. The ultimate bearing capacity of the foundation (in kPa, round off to 2 decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Shallow Foundations (Bearing Capacity)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Square footing width, \(B = 2\) m
    • Footing depth, \(D_f = 0\) (rests on the surface)
    • Cohesion, \(c = 24\) kPa
    • Angle of internal friction, \(\phi = 25°\)
    • Unit weight of soil, \(\gamma = 18\) kN/m³
    • General shear failure factors: \(N_c = 25.1\), \(N_q = 12.7\), \(N_\gamma = 9.7\)
    • Local shear failure factors: \(N_c' = 14.8\), \(N_q' = 5.6\), \(N_\gamma' = 3.2\)
  • Aim: Ultimate bearing capacity (\(q_u\)) in kPa.

3. Core Concepts:

Mode of Shear Failure Assessment:

  • \(\phi > 36°\) → General Shear Failure
  • \(\phi < 28°\) → Local Shear Failure

Since \(\phi = 25°\), the foundation will undergo Local Shear Failure.

Modified Soil Parameters: For local shear failure, mobilized cohesion \(c_m = \dfrac{2}{3}c\). The primed bearing capacity factors (\(N_c', N_q', N_\gamma'\)) must be used.

Terzaghi's Ultimate Bearing Capacity Equation for a Square Footing:

\[q_u = 1.3\, c_m N_c' + \bar{q}\, N_q' + 0.4\, \gamma\, B\, N_\gamma' \]

where \(\bar{q} = \gamma \times D_f\).

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate local shear mobilized parameters\[c_m = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 24 = 16\text{ kPa} \]Since \(D_f = 0\): \(\bar{q} = 0\).
  2. Step 2: Substitute values into Terzaghi's square footing equation\[q_u = (1.3 \times 16 \times 14.8) + 0 + (0.4 \times 18 \times 2 \times 3.2) \]
  3. Step 3: Final arithmetic computation
    • Cohesion component: \(1.3 \times 16 \times 14.8 = 307.84\) kPa
    • Width component: \(0.4 \times 18 \times 2 \times 3.2 = 46.08\) kPa
    \[q_u = 307.84 + 46.08 = 353.92\text{ kPa} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 353.92 kPa | Accepted key range: 350.00 to 355.00
